summary: Specifies a padding convention for the AES Key Wrap algorithm of RFC 3394, allowing keys of any practical length to be wrapped, not just multiples of 64 bits. It is informational.

eli5.summary: Key Wrap needs boxes of a certain size. This adds filler so keys of any size fit in.

subtitle: A padding convention that lets AES Key Wrap protect keys of any practical length, not just multiples of 64 bits.

tldr.problem: AES Key Wrap requires the key data to be two or more 64-bit blocks, so keys whose length is not a multiple of 64 bits cannot be wrapped.
tldr.mechanism: The key data is padded on the right with zero octets to a multiple of 8 octets. An Alternative Initial Value holding the constant A65959A6 and the original length in octets lets the receiver check integrity and strip the padding.
tldr.outcome: Keys from one octet up to 2^32 octets can be wrapped with a 128, 192 or 256 bit AES key-encryption key. The padded and unpadded algorithms use different constants, so one cannot be mistaken for the other.

today: RFC 5649 is an Informational RFC, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It builds on the AES Key Wrap algorithm of RFC 3394.

sections.title: The Problem with Odd-Sized Keys
sections.content:
Key wrapping means using one symmetric key to encrypt and integrity-protect another key, which can be symmetric or asymmetric. The AES Key Wrap algorithm of RFC 3394 needs its input, the key data, to be a sequence of two or more 64-bit blocks.

RFC 5649 extends it so a key of any practical size can be wrapped with an AES key-encryption key (KEK) of 128, 192 or 256 bits. The key data may be as short as one octet, giving an output of two 64-bit blocks (16 octets). A 32-bit field carries the octet length, which bounds the input at 2^32 octets, although most systems will have other limits well below that.
sections.eli5: A key-wrapping box only takes pieces in one fixed size. This document adds filler so a key that is a bit too short still fits the box.

sections.title: The Alternative Initial Value
sections.content:
The Alternative Initial Value (AIV) is 64 bits. Its high-order 32 bits are the constant A65959A6, which differs from the default IV of the original algorithm, so the two cannot be confused. Its low-order 32 bits are the message length indicator (MLI): an unsigned integer equal to the octet length of the plaintext key data, most significant octet first.

If the length is not a multiple of 8, the key data is padded on the right with the fewest zero octets needed to reach a multiple of 8. For a given number of 64-bit blocks only eight MLI values are possible. For example, with four blocks the valid values are 32 down to 25.

On unwrapping, three checks are made on the register A and the output of n blocks: the high 32 bits equal A65959A6; 8*(n-1) is less than the low 32 bits, which are at most 8*n; and the rightmost b octets of the output, where b is 8*n minus the MLI, are all zero. If any check fails, unwrapping MUST return an error.
sections.eli5: A label on the box says how long the real key is. The receiver reads the label, checks it makes sense, and throws away the filler.

sections.title: Wrapping and Unwrapping
sections.content:
To wrap, take m octets of key data, pad with zeros to r octets (the smallest multiple of 8 not less than m), and split into n = CEILING(m/8) blocks. If there is exactly one block, the AIV and the block form one 128-bit value that is encrypted with AES in ECB mode, giving two output blocks. Otherwise the wrapping process of RFC 3394 is applied to the padded blocks with the AIV as the initial value, giving n+1 blocks.

To unwrap, a single-block case is decrypted as one AES block to recover the AIV and the padded key. Otherwise steps 1 and 2 of the RFC 3394 unwrapping process are used, and the check of the A value is delayed until the AIV verification, because the padded plaintext is needed for it. After verification, the padding is removed using the length in the MLI.
sections.eli5: To pack, add filler until the key fills whole boxes, then lock them with the length label. To unpack, unlock, check the label and remove the filler.

sections.title: Identifiers and Examples
sections.content:
For protocols that use ASN.1, one algorithm identifier is assigned per KEK size: id-aes128-wrap-pad is { aes 8 }, id-aes192-wrap-pad is { aes 28 } and id-aes256-wrap-pad is { aes 48 }. The AlgorithmIdentifier parameter field MUST be absent. The appendices give ASN.1 modules for these identifiers.

The RFC includes two worked examples in hexadecimal using a 192-bit KEK: one wraps 20 octets of key data and the other wraps 7 octets.
sections.eli5: Each size of lock gets its own official name tag so programs can say which one they used. Two sample runs show what the answer should look like.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Implementations must protect the KEK, because its compromise can disclose every key wrapped with it. The KEK must be at least as good as the keying material it protects, and the effective security is that of the weaker algorithm. For example, a 128-bit AES key wrapped with a 256-bit AES key gives at most 128 bits of protection.

The padded and unpadded algorithms use different constants in the initial value, so padded key data cannot be unwrapped as unpadded data or the reverse. This stays true even when no padding is needed. The padded algorithm gives almost the same integrity protection as the original. System designers should not use these algorithms to encrypt anything other than cryptographic keying material.
sections.eli5: Guard the master lock, because it opens every wrapped key. A chain is only as strong as its weakest link, and use key-wrapping only for keys.

fields.name: Constant
fields.desc: Fixed constant, high-order half of the AIV.

fields.name: MLI
fields.desc: Octet length of the plaintext key data, most significant octet first.
